---
title: "5.2 Applications of Bernoulli"
---

{{< include ../_checkpoint-widget.qmd >}}

## The big idea

Last reading we derived Bernoulli's Equation, but we are more interested in **applying it to engineering problems** — that is what we're doing today.

We'll start with three applications, each involving Bernoulli's Equation — and two of the three will also lean on a statement of conservation of mass. 

- One is about pipe flow: **the Venturi Nozzle** is a section of pipe that is narrowed, which (as Bernoulli tells us) reduces the pressure. The reduced pressure gives design opportunities to, e.g., draw chemicals into the flow, but in this reading we'll talk about using it to measure flow speed.
- One is about external flow: **the Pitot Tube** is a device for measuring the speed of an aircraft, again based on the relationship between pressure and velocity. There are some important vocabulary words here too: static and stagnation pressure.
- One is on a jet: **the tank and jet** problem concerns draining a tank of fluid through an open faucet. The interesting question is: how long does it take to drain? Conservation of mass will serve as a differential equation here!


## Think first

**Recall**

1. Bernoulli's Equation! $p+\frac12 \rho U^2 +\rho g z =\text{ constant}$.
2. Conservation of mass! $\dot{m}\equiv \rho U A = \text{ constant}$.

**Look ahead**

1. Double the pressure difference you measure across a Venturi nozzle. Does the flow rate through it double?
2. A Pitot tube has two holes: one pointed straight into the wind, one on the side of the probe. Why does it need both — wouldn't the front one alone tell you the speed?
3. Two tanks are filled to the same depth, one 2 m wide, and the other 2 cm wide. Out of identical faucets at the bottom, which jet comes out faster? Which tank empties first?

We have flow from left to right that passes from a wide cross section (area $A_1$) to a narrower cross section ($A_2$) (and then back to a wide wide cross section again). We assume uniform flow speeds $U_1$ and $U_2$ and pressures $p_1$ and $p_2$ are measured. From Bernoulli, we expect $p_1 > p_2$.

Some motivation: It is difficult to measure a flow speed directly — e.g., we could put a vane or other obstacle in the way, but that is going to change the flow or will necessitate extra pumping power to achieve the same velocity as without the obstacle. Meanwhile, it is easy to measure pressure. So: **let's use the pressure measurements, as well as the known geometry, to calculate the flow speed**.


::: {.column-margin}
Measure pressure by: attaching a plate with known area to a spring, then measure the displacement of the spring:

$$
F_\text{spring} = k \Delta x \implies p = \frac{k \Delta x}{A}.
$$
:::






**Step 0:** Confirm that Bernoulli's Equation is applicable. Reminder: it applies in cases where it is **safe to ignore viscosity**, which can be checked with a Reynolds number calculation; and we need to be able to connect two points via a streamline.




**Step 1:** Identify two states that can be connected by Bernoulli's Equation. In this problem, we'll connect the center of the tube upstream ("1") to the center of the throat ("2"), and these can definitely be joined by a streamline. Write

$$
p_1 + \frac12 \rho U_1^2 + \rho g z_1 = p_2 + \frac12 \rho U_2^2 + \rho g z_2.
$$


**Step 2:** Simplify the equation with reasonable assumptions. Here, we know there will be different speeds and pressures at "1" and "2", and all that information is relevant. But we also recognize $z_1=z_2$. With this consideration we can write 

$$
p_1 + \frac12 \rho U_1^2 = p_2+ \frac12 \rho U_2^2.
$$

**Step 3:** Take stock and look for additional information. This is one equation, two unknowns... we don't know either velocity. So we need to come up with another equation.

Think about **conservation of mass**: all the mass passing through location "1" must also pass through location "2", and so

$$
\dot{m}=\text{constant} = \rho U_1 A_1 = \rho U_2 A_2.
$$

Another way to phrase this is

$$
U_1 = \frac{\dot{m}}{\rho A_1} \qquad \text{and} \qquad U_2 = \frac{\dot{m}}{\rho A_2}.
$$

::: {.column-margin}
At this point we have three equations and three unknowns: we don't know $\dot{m}$ yet.
:::

**Step 4:** Complete the math. Grouping the pressure terms together, and the velocity terms together, and then substituting in $\dot{m}$, we find

$$
p_1 - p_2= \frac12 \rho \left(\left(\frac{\dot{m}}{\rho A_2}\right)^2-\left(\frac{\dot{m}}{\rho A_1}\right)^2\right)
= \frac{\dot{m}^2}{2\rho}\left(\frac{1}{A_2^2}-\frac{1}{A_1^2}\right)
$$

and can solve for

$$
\dot{m}= \sqrt{\dfrac{2\rho\left(p_1-p_2\right)}{\dfrac{1}{A_2^2}-\dfrac{1}{A_1^2}}}.
$$

That is: we can determine the mass flow rate from the known geometry and two easily-measured pressures.

::: {.column-margin}
We might instead report the volumetric flow rate $Q = \dot{m}/\rho$, or actually calculate the velocity $U_1 = \dot{m}/(\rho A_1)$.
:::

**Step 5:** is the answer reasonable? This equation tells us that the larger the pressure difference, the bigger the mass flow rate. That makes sense: bigger pressure drop, bigger "push", more flow. We could also [check the units](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=%281+m%5E2%29%281+m%5E2%29+sqrt%28%281+kg%2Fm%5E3%29*%281+Pa%29%2F%281+m%5E2%29%5E2%29).



## Pitot Tube

A similar device for external flows: [the Pitot tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitot_tube). These are common devices on planes for measuring airspeed — again, it is difficult to measure speed in this situation without adding an extra obstacle to flow... and there are some pretty dire consequences if you ruin the aerodynamics of an airplane!

::: {.column-margin}
In fluid mechanics we refer to "internal flows" — flows *through* pipes and ducts — and "external flows" — flows *over* spheres and cars.
:::

Here is a cross-section:

```

The idea: at the "nose" (point "1"), incoming flow must decide whether to go above, or below, or left, or right of that point. As a consequence, we can claim that the velocity there is zero — we call this a stagnation point. On the bottom of this device, at point "2", flow passes over a small hole. In both positions "1" and "2" we are able to make a pressure measurement — we call the pressure at "1" the **stagnation pressure** and at "2" the **static pressure**.


::: {.callout-tip}
The **static pressure** is the pressure that would actually be measured by a device... arguably it is "the pressure".
:::


So: what does Bernoulli tell us? Technically points "1" and "2" are *not* on the same streamline — but the oncoming flow is uniform and the height difference between those streamlines is negligible. So the "Bernoulli constant" is the same on both streamlines, and we can connect across them. Writing out the full equation

$$
p_1 + \frac12 \rho U_1^2 + \rho g z_1 = p_2 + \frac12 \rho U_2^2 + \rho g z_2
$$

we simplify with the assumptions that $z_1\approx z_2$ and that $U_1 = 0$. After a bit of rearranging, we arrive at

$$
U = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\rho}\left(p_\text{stagnation} - p_\text{static}\right)}
$$

where we have renamed $p_1=p_\text{stagnation}$, $p_2=p_\text{static}$, and $U_2=U$ is the air speed. Again: we are able to make a velocity measurement based on two pressure measurements.


::: {.callout-note}
Why did we not need conservation of mass here?
:::


## Tank and jet

We need to do a quick aside.

### The other component of Bernoulli's Equation

Recall that we examined $\sum F_s = ma_s$ to derive Bernoulli's Equation. We can also look at the normal components, and a similar derivation would reveal

$$
\rho \frac{U_s^2}{\mathcal{R}} = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial n} - \rho g \frac{\partial z}{\partial n}
$$

where $\mathcal{R}$ is the radius of curvature of the streamline and the normal coordinate $n$ always points towards the center of the curvature.

::: {.column-margin}
If a streamline was following a circle with radius $R$, its radius of curvature is $\mathcal{R}=R$.
:::

There are some important consequences of this, one of which: if we neglect gravity, and **if the streamlines are straight, the pressure in each cross-section of the flow is the same**.



::: {.callout-tip}
Another interesting consequence: if we imagine a collection of streamlines circling the origin, we'll have $\partial p/\partial n < 0$. This means that, as we increase our $n$-coordinate (i.e., move towards the center of the curvature/of the rotation), the pressure will decrease. Tornadoes have a low-pressure center!
:::

  <!-- the thing we actually want -->
  <text x="470" y="330" font-size="16" fill="#2b6ca3" xml:space="preserve">
    <tspan font-style="italic">U</tspan><tspan font-size="11" dy="4">jet</tspan><tspan font-size="16" dy="-4"> = ?</tspan>
  </text>
</svg>
</div>
```

We have a tank with cross-section $A_\text{tank}$ holding a fluid of density $\rho$, open on the top. At the bottom of the tank is a faucet with cross-section $A_\text{jet}$... when the faucet is open, a jet is produced. The classic problem is: How long does it take to drain the tank?

We choose the first state (which we'll go ahead and label with "tank") to be the top surface of the fluid, and the "jet" state to be within the jet, just outside the faucet. then write Bernoulli's Equation:

$$
p_\text{tank} + \frac12 \rho U_\text{tank}^2 + \rho g z_\text{tank} = p_\text{jet} + \frac12 \rho U_\text{jet}^2 + \rho g z_\text{jet}.
$$


::: {.callout-tip}
How do we know to use these two points? For the jet side, we have information that is going to be useful: if we know the speed that the fluid leaves the tank, we can figure out the time it takes to drain. On the tank side, we can reasonably claim to know some relevant information here: we know the surface elevation relative to the jet, we know the pressure (zero gauge pressure), and we can assume that the speed of the surface is very slow such that the kinetic energy is negligible.
:::



We have the freedom to define $z=0$ wherever we like... *all that matters is the elevation change*. Let's say $z=0=z_\text{jet}$, and call $z_\text{tank}=H$. 

We also note that **both pressures** are zero (gauge). The pressure on the jet side is harder to rationalize, but note: the air on the outside of the jet is at zero gauge pressure, and from our above aside, we might assume that the jet leaves as a uniform straight flow such that the pressure change normal to the flow direction is zero. Thus, it is reasonable to assume $p_\text{jet}\appro 0$.

Here is what Bernoulli simplifies to:

$$
\frac12 \rho U_\text{tank}^2 + \rho g H = \frac12 \rho U_\text{jet}^2.
$$

We'll make one more assumption: that the tank's surface is moving slowly such that its kinetic energy is negligible. In such a case we can write

$$
\rho g H = \frac12 \rho U_\text{jet}^2
$$

and rearrange to say

$$
U_\text{jet} = \sqrt{2g H}.
$$

This is an important result! The speed of a jet is related to the height of the water above the jet. We are essentially converting potential energy into kinetic energy.

Definitely interesting, but our original question was: How long does it take to drain the tank? This equation doesn't really answer it... when the tank is at zero height, the jet has zero speed, great.

We need to look for another avenue to figure out how to get the draining time. And... it's going to involve calculus! What happens when we look at the conservation of mass? We can write

$$
\rho U_\text{tank} A_\text{tank} = \rho U_\text{jet} A_\text{jet}
$$

and then cancel-out $\rho$ and bring-in $H$ into $U_\text{jet}$

$$
U_\text{tank} A_\text{tank} = \sqrt{2gH}A_\text{jet}.
$$


::: {.callout-note}
In Bernoulli's Equation, we neglected the term that included $U_\text{tank}$ claiming it was small. What happens if we do the same with this equation? We end up with $U_\text{jet}=0$ as well!

In Bernoulli's equation, there were three terms in the equation and we could reasonably claim that one of those three terms was smaller than the other two. In conservation of mass, there are only two terms, and so the two terms must balance each other.


:::


One equation, two unknowns: $U_\text{tank}$ and $H$. But actually... look at the picture above. Does it make sense that $U_\text{tank} = - dH/dt$? Stare at it til it does!


::: {.callout-caution}
If you forget the negative sign, there will be issues: $dH/dt$ is a negative number!
:::

Plugging this in, we can arrive at

$$
-\frac{dH}{dt}A_\text{tank} = \sqrt{2gH} A_\text{jet}
$$

a little differential equation. It is separable, meaning we can rewrite it as

$$
\frac{dH}{\sqrt{2gH}} = -\frac{A_\text{jet}}{A_\text{tank}} dt
$$

and then integrate both sides

$$
\frac{2}{\sqrt{2g}}\sqrt{H} = - \frac{A_\text{jet}}{A_\text{tank}} t + \text{ constant}.
$$

To determine the constant we suppose that we know an "initial condition": at $t=0$, the height is $H_0$.

Plugging this information in tells us that the constant is $2\sqrt{H_0}/\sqrt{2g}$, and so we can find

$$
t = \frac{A_\text{tank}}{A_\text{jet}}\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{2g}}\sqrt{H_0}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2g}}\sqrt{H}\right).
$$

This is **a function for the time it takes to reach a height of $H$**, and so we can immediately determine the time it takes to reach a height of $H=0$:

$$
t_\text{empty}= \frac{A_\text{tank}}{A_\text{jet}}\sqrt{2H_0/g}.
$$
